doc.title: Hal Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: A tense concert where a star demanded loud drumming
summary: An unnamed headliner stopped the tune and told him to play like in a 200-piece band, though others like Doc Cheatham and Milt Hinton make up for it.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Did you ever have a circumstance where it’s been like a train wreck?
Yes. Are you sure you want to think about that? And is it usually something inherent in the rhythm section that’s not, like you said, someone’s trying to dominate or just not —

No. Because I haven’t had many train wrecks with rhythm sections. It’s been the horn players, who’ll tell you one thing and then they forgot they told you that. Or, they want to control the rhythm section. It wasn’t a train wreck, but it was a very nerve wracking experience, I played with an individual who shall remain nameless, who was feature- billed with another Swing Era musician who shall also remain nameless. And there was a slight battle of the egos before the concert and it translated into telling the rhythm section how to play. And nothing we did was right. And one of these guys has written extensively about Dave Tough, who is one of my great heroes on the drums, and I thought here’s my chance — Dave Tough, that’s what I’m going to do all night. So I tried to play real subtly on the first tune, and he waves it to a halt and he said, “Play like you’re playing in a 200-piece band.”
Oh, wow. He stopped the tune and did that?

So I did. I played like I was building a house. And that’s what he wanted. But then I heard another concert later where he was complaining about, “All drummers are house builders.” I was only following orders.
What are you going to do? But then, for every experience like that there’s Doc Cheatham, or Milt Hinton. And you walk off the bandstand thinking boy I’m glad I did that. So they make up for it.
